text: {"answer":"The passages mostly suggest that minimum wage increases produce only modest employment losses, though the evidence is not uniform. A synthesis of meta-analyses reports that the own-wage employment elasticity is consistently modest, so job losses are limited relative to wage gains, and that corrected estimates after accounting for publication bias generally approach zero [3ed11781c282#1][3ed11781c282#0]. An IESE analysis of US data from 2010 to 2016 finds that in concentrated labor markets a hike can raise employment, while in markets with many employers the effect is neutral or slightly negative [cb6fd29ac7f5#1][cb6fd29ac7f5#3][cb6fd29ac7f5#4]. A Spanish machine-learning study over 2001 to 2021 reports that increases were consistent with higher net employment, though it is a single country and focuses on inequality [6bc17d95795b#1]. On the other side, an advocacy-linked brief from the Employment Policies Institute states that the majority of research over three decades finds that minimum wage increases reduce employment [4314fdf0529f#0]. That source is from an organization with a policy stake, and its claim is a general summary rather than a cited study.
